```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(cfbstats)
library(dplyr)
library(targets)
root <- cfbstats_root()
if (nzchar(root)) {
  knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = root)
}
```

Interactive exemplars for the three chart families the project uses: **time
series**, **2D**, and **3D**. Each reads a pipeline target, so the input → chart
lineage is explicit. The default stack is R htmlwidgets (`plotly`, `ggiraph`);
Observable JS is reserved for bespoke explorables (a later addition).

```{r}
#| label: data
picks <- tar_read(picks) |>
  filter(year >= 2013, !is.na(height), !is.na(weight), !is.na(overall))
```

## Time series — drafts per year

```{r}
#| label: fig-timeseries
viz_drafts_by_season(tar_read(model_table))
```

## 2D — draft capital vs. physicals (hover for player)

Each point is a drafted player; hover for the name. Color encodes draft round.

```{r}
#| label: fig-2d
viz_scatter_2d(
  dplyr::slice_sample(picks, n = min(1500, nrow(picks))),
  x = weight,
  y = height,
  tooltip = name,
  color = round
)
```

## 3D — height × weight × overall pick

```{r}
#| label: fig-3d
viz_scatter_3d(
  picks,
  x = "height",
  y = "weight",

)
```

## NFL outcomes — how long drafted players last

Each point is a drafted player bridged to nflverse (decision 0014), placed by
draft round against the number of distinct **seasons they spent on an NFL
roster** — the project's primary longevity measure. The **#1 overall picks** are
highlighted against the rest of the field; the grey bar marks each round's
median. Hover for the player. Recent draft classes are still active, so their
counts are **right-censored** lower bounds.

```{r}
#| label: fig-nfl-longevity
viz_nfl_roster_seasons_by_round(tar_read(picks_nfl), tar_read(nfl_rosters))
```

## Career length — how long is a college career?

Each player's career is summarized from the **roster backbone** — distinct
seasons on a roster per athlete id, including seasons with no stat line. The
shape of this distribution is the baseline every other career question is read
against: most careers are short, so a fifth or sixth season is already a
distinct population, and how long a player stayed in college plausibly shapes
both their development and their draft odds. Gap seasons (years absent between
first and last appearance) are also recorded here — they are the raw material
for the injury-shaped-gap analysis below. Hover a bar for the player count.

```{r}
#| label: fig-career-length
viz_career_length(tar_read(roster))
```

::: {.callout-note}
A long career is not always continuous: a fifth or sixth season can be a
redshirt year, a medical hardship, or a COVID-era extension, and the roster
grain cannot separate them. The next section formalizes what *can* be inferred
about redshirts from this data — approximately, and with an explicit
confound.
:::

## Redshirts — what the data can and cannot say

A **redshirt** is an NCAA eligibility designation: a player spends a season on
a roster **without competing in it**, and that season does not count against
their four seasons of eligibility — they effectively gain a fifth (sometimes
sixth) year. Since 2018 a redshirted player may still appear in up to four
games without burning the redshirt, so "played a little" and "redshirted" are
no longer mutually exclusive. No feed in this project labels who redshirted,
so it must be **inferred** — approximately — from two signals:

1. **Stat-gap shape** — a roster season with **no stat line that the player
   returned from**. Here a *stat line* means any recorded season statistic for
   that player-season in the `player_stats` table — a pass attempt, a tackle,
   a reception, anything. Having **no** stat line is our best available proxy
   for "did not compete". The "returned from" guard matters: a final-year
   absence is just as likely an injury or an early departure as a redshirt,
   so it is never flagged.
2. **Fifth-year class** — appearing at eligibility class 5, one year beyond
   the nominal four-year window.

Both flags are *redshirt-shaped*, not certified, for three reasons. First, a
no-stat season is not proof of non-participation: a deep-bench player can
appear in games without recording a statistic, a season can end early to
injury, and (pre-2018 rules) even four appearances disqualify a redshirt while
still producing a thin stat line. Second, a class-5 player may be a grad
transfer or junior-college arrival rather than a redshirt. Third — and most
consequential here — whether a stat line exists at all depends on how
completely the source records statistics, and it records them for well under
half of roster seasons in the early years. The second chart below is built to
make exactly that visible.

```{r}
#| label: redshirt-setup
#| include: false
# Redshirt flags are pipeline targets (decision 0021) — no recomputation here.
flagged <- tar_read(roster_flags)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-redshirt-career
#| fig-width: 9
viz_redshirt_by_career_length(flagged)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-redshirt-seasonality
#| fig-width: 9
viz_redshirt_seasonality(flagged)
```

The seasonality chart reads like a ledger for each season: grey is what we
*know* (a stat line exists, so the player competed), teal is what the flag
claims (no stats, came back), and amber is what we deliberately refuse to
judge (no stats in a final season). Two things stand out. First, grey grows
from about a quarter of roster seasons in 2010–2015 to around 60% by 2021 —
the source did not record stats for most players in the early years at all,
which is why the teal share there (45–48%) is dominated by missing data rather
than redshirts. Second, even in the best-covered seasons teal runs ~25%:
that is an **upper bound** on redshirting, mixing true redshirts with bench
players who never recorded a statistic. The teal share only becomes
meaningfully comparable *across* seasons with similar grey shares, which is
roughly 2016 onward (2020's bump reflects COVID-era eligibility rules and a
shortened stat season). The career-length split above should be read the same
way: descriptive of the flag, never a certified redshirt rate.

## Movement — transfers

College players change schools more than they used to — the transfer portal has
made it routine — and *where* a player moves matters as much as *that* they
move: a jump from a Group-of-Five program to a Power-Five roster is a different
bet than a lateral move within the same tier. This section counts team changes
by season and splits each move by **tier direction**: `up` means the move went
to a higher conference tier (e.g. G5 → Power), where direction is evaluated
against the season-aware tier of each school, so conference realignment is read
against the season of the move rather than a fixed conference list. Hover a
segment for the count.

Counts come from the player-season change features (stat-line players). The
career-grain rate below — computed on the full roster backbone — is the share
of players whose career included **at least one** transfer; together the two
views answer how common movement is, when it clusters (rule changes, portal
eras), and whether it tends to be upward.

```{r}
#| label: fig-transfers
viz_transfers_by_season(tar_read(ps_change))
```

```{r}
#| label: transfer-rate
rate <- transfer_rate(tar_read(career))
```

Of the `r format(rate$players, big.mark = ",")` players on rosters,
`r format(rate$transferred, big.mark = ",")`
(`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * rate$share)`) changed teams at least once.

::: {.callout-note}
Both views undercount subtly: the per-season counts only cover players with a
stat line, and neither view sees a transfer whose origin season has no roster
row. A gap-season move (sit out, then appear elsewhere) still counts, because
the direction compares to the prior *observed* season.
:::

## Player dossier

`player_dossier()` resolves a player's scattered rows into one **interpreted**
record (decision 0019) rather than a raw extract that is easy to misread. Each
dossier shows: identity and physicals; college statistics grouped and labeled by
game **phase** (offense / defense / special teams); per-season coaching context;
name-guarded high-school recruiting; the NFL outcome (drafted or
undrafted-signed) with longevity; and a provenance / caveats block.

Below are the **#1 overall picks of the past five NFL drafts**, each rendered as
an interpreted dossier.

Notes:

- A bare `TD` in the long `player_stats` is ambiguous, so stats are relabelled
  by phase (e.g. "Passing touchdowns" vs "Defensive touchdowns").
- A blank coach cell is shown as "head coach not available" — the CFBD coaches
  feed is FBS head coaches only, so a non-FBS season (e.g. Cam Ward's 2021 FCS
  year at Incarnate Word) is flagged, not silently dropped.
- Recruiting is name-guarded (decision 0013); a genuinely unrated player stays
  unrated, never imputed.
- NFL longevity is **right-censored** for these recent picks — all are still
  active, so seasons/games are lower bounds.

```{r}
#| label: dossier-setup
#| include: false
# Read the shared inputs once; `dossier()` keys a player by CFBD athlete id.
ps <- tar_read(player_stats)
ros <- tar_read(roster)
co <- tar_read(coaches)
picks_nfl <- tar_read(picks_nfl)
rec <- tar_read(recruiting)
nrs <- tar_read(nfl_rosters)
nps <- tar_read(nfl_player_stats)
dossier <- function(id) {
  player_dossier(id, ps, ros, co, picks_nfl, rec, nrs, nps)
}
```

### Fernando Mendoza — 2026 #1, Indiana


## Branding — team logos

The `teams` dimension carries each program's logo and colors, joined by school
name via `link_team_meta()` and kept off the model path (display only, decision
0008). Two rendering paths: a `reactable` table with logo thumbnails and color
swatches, and a `ggiraph` bar filled with each team's brand color that shows its
logo on hover.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-team-logos
viz_team_logos(tar_read(teams))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-drafts-by-team
viz_drafts_by_team(tar_read(model_table), tar_read(teams))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
These are templates, not findings — they demonstrate the wiring from a pipeline
target to an interactive widget. Real analyses will pair model inputs with model
results on the same page.
:::
